milestone.title: Apple sells the one-millionth Apple II
milestone.note: On July 18, the Apple II family reached one million sales, a landmark for the personal-computer industry.

lead.headline: Apple II Sales Reach One Million
lead.dek: Six years after its debut, the expandable 6502 machine crosses a landmark that shows how far personal computing has moved beyond the hobby bench.
body: Apple Computer sold its one-millionth Apple II on July 18, giving the personal-computer business a round-number milestone few could have imagined when the original machine appeared in 1977. The figure belongs to the whole Apple II family, whose color graphics, expansion slots, and accessible design carried it from enthusiasts’ rooms into schools, offices, and neighborhood computer shops.

The achievement is also a victory for continuity. While rivals repeatedly introduced incompatible machines, Apple kept the 6502-based line recognizable and useful, allowing owners to build libraries of disks, peripherals, and skills. Thousands of programs and a broad dealer network turned the computer into a platform rather than a one-season appliance.

That installed base now feeds a self-reinforcing market. Software houses can justify ambitious releases because so many customers own compatible machines; buyers can justify the hardware because shelves are crowded with business tools, educational titles, utilities, and games. Expansion cards further let an Apple II grow with its owner instead of being discarded.

One million machines does not settle the home-computer contest. Commodore’s aggressive prices and the swelling ranks of lower-cost systems are changing shoppers’ expectations. But this week’s milestone confirms that the personal computer has become a durable mass-market category—and that software may be the next battleground.

stories.headline: Commodore Threatens to Halve Software Prices
stories.dek: The hardware price war may be coming to cartridges and disks.
body: Personal Computer News reports that Commodore is pressing for a $99 ceiling on software and considering mass-market cartridges priced as low as $10 to $15. Such figures would cut sharply against premium packages and extend Commodore’s familiar hardware tactics into publishing.

Lower prices could put more titles into ordinary retail channels and tempt owners to buy more often, but they would also squeeze developers and dealers. The proposal makes clear that the contest for home-computer buyers will be fought as much on software shelves as at the hardware counter.

stories.headline: Whole Earth Maps a 40,000-Program Jungle
stories.dek: Stewart Brand turns cataloging instincts toward an exploding, confusing market.
body: TIME describes Stewart Brand’s effort to bring order to a software market estimated at roughly 40,000 programs. His Whole Earth Software Catalog would mix descriptions, criticism, and practical recommendations for buyers facing a bewildering range of products.

Brand planned to tap dial-up communities, including EIES, for recommendations—an early sign that computer networks could become engines of software word of mouth. The project recognizes a new industry problem: abundance has arrived faster than trustworthy guidance.

stories.headline: More Memory for Less in the Home-Computer War
stories.dek: Sub-$100 machines and rumors of IBM’s “Peanut” crowd the summer market.
body: COMPUTE! surveys a market in which falling prices no longer mean toy specifications. Commodore’s pressure and new Atari models are forcing makers to offer more memory and capability at prices that would have seemed impossible only a short time ago.

The magazine also relays expectations of an IBM home machine near $600. That “Peanut” remains rumor—the PCjr will not be announced until November—but its prominence shows how seriously established computer companies now regard the household buyer.
